title: Hamsa Emoji 🪬 Meaning: The Protective Hand Explained
description: The hamsa emoji 🪬 is a protective hand amulet, called the Hand of Fatima or Hand of Miriam. Learn what it means across cultures and how it differs from the nazar 🧿.
summary: 🪬 is the hamsa, a palm-shaped amulet used for protection against the evil eye and for blessings and good fortune. It is shared across Middle Eastern and North African cultures and in Jewish and Muslim traditions. Online, people add it to good news, new homes, babies and wishes for safety.
meaning: The hamsa is an open right hand, usually drawn with a thumb on each side so it looks symmetrical, and often an eye set in the palm. The name comes from the word for five in Arabic, khamsa, a reference to the fingers; Hebrew speakers sometimes call it a hamesh hand for the same reason. Hung on walls, doors and necklaces, it is meant to keep away harm and envy.

Several faiths and cultures claim it as their own, and each has a name for it. In Muslim communities, especially across North Africa, it is often called the Hand of Fatima, after the daughter of the Prophet Muhammad. In Jewish communities it is known as the Hand of Miriam, after the sister of Moses and Aaron, and it is particularly familiar among Sephardic and Mizrahi families. Some Christians in the region call it the Hand of Mary.

On screens, the emoji does what the amulet does. People attach 🪬 to announcements that could attract envy: a pregnancy, an engagement, a new car, an exam passed. It also serves as a quiet sign of heritage for people of Moroccan, Tunisian, Lebanese, Israeli, Iraqi or other backgrounds where the hamsa is a household object.

Wellness and spiritual accounts also use it more loosely as a symbol of protection, positive energy and personal boundaries, placing it alongside crystals, moons and the evil eye bead. Its meaning there is general and not tied to a particular religion. Jewelry and home decor brands use it in the same spirit, which is part of why the shape is recognized far beyond the communities where it began.

contexts.label: In captions
contexts.body: The hamsa often closes a post about a blessing: a new baby, a new house, a business opening, a recovery. It works like a written “protect this,” asking that the good news not be spoiled. Some people pair it with 🧿 for double protection, a combination that mirrors jewelry where the two appear together.

contexts.label: Around the world
contexts.body: It is common in Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Egypt, Lebanon, Israel and across the Jewish and Arab diasporas, often as wall decor or a necklace. Tourist markets sell it widely, which has spread its look far beyond its origins. For many families it is a specific heirloom, not just a decorative pattern.

contexts.label: In texting
contexts.body: Friends and relatives send 🪬 as a blessing in reply to good news, much like saying “may it be protected” or “no evil eye.” It also appears before travel, surgery or exams as a wish for safety. Among older relatives it can be a warm, almost parental gesture.

confusedWith.difference: 🧿 is the blue nazar bead, a round eye charm associated especially with Turkey and Greece. 🪬 is a hand-shaped amulet. Both guard against the evil eye and are often worn together, but they are distinct objects.
✋ is an ordinary raised palm for stop, high five or volunteering. The hamsa has a symmetrical shape, often with an eye in the palm, and carries a protective, spiritual meaning.
🙏 means please, thank you or prayer across many contexts. 🪬 is narrower: a specific amulet for protection and blessing in Middle Eastern, Jewish and Muslim traditions.

avoid: Do not use it as a joke or mockery of religious belief, since it is a meaningful symbol for many Jewish and Muslim families.
Avoid presenting it as belonging to only one religion or culture when talking to a mixed audience; it is shared across several.
design: The emoji shows an upright hand with fingers together and a thumb shape on both sides, giving it a mirror-image outline. Most designs are blue, sometimes with gold or white accents, and many include a small eye or decorative circle at the center of the palm. It resembles the amulets sold as pendants and wall hangings.

faqs.q: Is the hamsa Jewish or Muslim?
faqs.a: Both, and more. It is used in Jewish communities as the Hand of Miriam and in Muslim communities as the Hand of Fatima, and the symbol is older than either name. Christians in the Middle East use it too. It is best understood as a shared regional symbol.

🪬 is a hand-shaped amulet, the hamsa, while 🧿 is a round blue eye bead, the nazar. Both protect against the evil eye, and the two are often combined, but they come from different traditions and look different.

faqs.q: Is it okay to use the hamsa emoji if I’m not from that culture?
faqs.a: Generally yes, when used respectfully as a wish for protection or blessing. It is widely used in jewelry and design. Avoid using it as a joke or in a way that treats a meaningful religious and cultural symbol as a meme.

faqs.q: When was the hamsa emoji added?
faqs.a: 🪬 was approved as part of emoji version 14.0 in 2021, and devices began showing it as their software updated over the following months. Before that, people used 🧿 or ✋ as a stand-in.
